st.headline: Malaysia’s growth tops forecasts as AI boom drives export surge
st.teaser: Gross domestic product rose 5.3% in the three months through September from a year earlier.
fullText: KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia’s economic growth slowed but still exceeded expectations as the artificial intelligence boom continued to bolster exports and domestic demand remained resilient.

Gross domestic product rose 5.3% in the three months through September from a year earlier, according to advance estimates from the Department of Statistics Malaysia on Oct 16, beating the 5.1% median prediction in a Bloomberg survey.
Third quarter growth, however, slowed from the 6% expansion in the previous three-month period.
Third quarter growth was underpinned by positive performance across most economic sectors, the department said in a statement.
Only the mining and quarrying sector contracted, it added.
The better-than-expected reading underscores the resilience of Malaysia’s economy even as growth moderates from a strong first half.
Robust domestic consumption and demand for electronics used in artificial intelligence have helped cushion the trade-dependent economy from disruptions caused by the US war against Iran .
The services sector rose 5.4%, bolstered by wholesale and retail trade, information and communication as well as finance, the statistics department said.
Manufacturing strengthened by 7.5%, backed in part by export-oriented industries, particularly electrical and electronic products.

Bank Negara Malaysia governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said in an interview this week that the economy is likely to grow about 5% in 2026, with the nation’s diverse sources of growth helping cushion it against any slowdown in the AI boom.
Malaysia’s economy grew 5.5% during the three quarters of 2026, the department said, above the government’s revised growth forecast of 4.8% to 5.3% for the year.
The government in October raised the forecast from 4% to 5% previously.
Household spending remains firm, as fuel subsidies helped shield consumers from elevated energy cost.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim earlier in October also announced more cash aid and a higher minimum wage for 2027 to ease cost-of-living pressures.
The government expects Malaysia’s economy to grow at 4.2% to 5.2% in 2027, supported by sustained domestic demand investment activity.
Preliminary GDP data, which will provide a detailed analysis of the third quarter, will be released on Nov 18. BLOOMBERG

cna.headline: NTU student creates website that estimates how many cigarettes’ worth of haze you've breathed in
cna.teaser: "I just wanted to craft a simple-looking website, as I have a few family members and friends that are also often overwhelmed by all the different numbers, and I just wanted a simple website for them to use," Zi Heng tells 8days.sg.
fullText: Everyone's been diligently checking PM2.5 readings before stepping outdoors these days. But one Singaporean has come up with a different metric to help people make sense of the haze.
Zi Heng, 21, a Data Science and Artificial Intelligence student at Nanyang Technological University (NTU), recently created a website called How Much Haze Have You Smoked Today?
The website estimates how many cigarettes' worth of fine-particle pollution one could have been exposed to based on Singapore's haze readings.

Speaking to 8days.sg, Zi Heng said: "I am a firm believer in not smoking. It does indeed feel ironic to equate the haze to cigarettes, but perhaps we should view the haze to be as dangerous as cigarettes, as I feel some youngsters might be underestimating the danger the haze brings."

The website’s measurements are based on metrics from environmental research organisation Berkeley Earth, which estimates that breathing air containing 22 micrograms of PM2.5 per cubic metre over 24 hours is roughly comparable to smoking one cigarette.

The calculation assumes someone is breathing outdoor air continuously at an average breathing rate. These are rough comparisons based on outdoor air pollution levels, not actual cigarettes smoked or a medical assessment of the health effects.

When 8days.sg checked the website on Oct 14 at 4pm, it estimated that the island-wide average PM2.5 exposure over the previous 24 hours was equivalent to 4.4 cigarettes. If the pollution level recorded during the latest hour were to continue for an entire day, the exposure could be equivalent to 9.4 cigarettes.
The idea behind the website was simple: Zi Heng just wanted to make haze readings easier to understand.

"I just wanted to craft a simple-looking website, as I have a few family members and friends that are also often overwhelmed by all the different numbers, so I just wanted a simple website for them to use," he added.
It took him just a week to build the website on his own, and he only decided to share it online after receiving positive feedback from family and friends.

"I find that the 24h PSI is a little like trying to drive a car while looking at the rear-view mirror and doesn't help with whether I should go for a run now," he explained. "The one-hour PM2.5 readings are also decent, but it is confusing because the scale of it differs from the 24h PSI."
His website displays one-hour and three-hour PSI estimates, calculated from PM2.5 concentrations, alongside NEA 's official 24-hour PSI readings.
It also breaks down air pollution levels across Singapore's north, south, east, west and central regions.
However, Zi Heng makes it clear that his one-hour and three-hour PSI figures are his own calculations, not official NEA readings.
"I have listed quite a lot of warnings near all my readings! The last thing I would want is to mislead anyone," he said.
The website also draws data directly from NEA's API.
According to Zi Heng, the data generally updates within one to two minutes of the start of each hour, while he has observed that NEA's public haze website sometimes takes around 10 minutes to update.
Zi Heng also stresses that the measurements should not be taken as medical advice.

"It shouldn't be used as a scientific measure or for advice, but it can hopefully help convince vulnerable people to stay home during the haze, just like they would avoid a smoking corner," he explained.
"I was really shocked by just how bad the haze is when putting it to a metric that we already know is bad conventionally (cigarettes)," he admitted.
What started as a personal project has since caught the attention of other Singaporeans after he shared it on Reddit, with the website attracting around 2,000 views daily as of Oct 14.
For now, he intends to keep the website running indefinitely, even after the haze clears.
And while the cigarette calculator may sound alarming, Zi Heng says the project is ultimately meant to give Singaporeans a different perspective on air pollution.
"It's just a little bit of fun, and I just want to provide a different way of viewing the same problem all of us Singaporeans are facing," he said.
And Zi Heng, who has never smoked, isn't encouraging anyone to start.
In fact, he revealed that the cigarette calculator wasn't originally meant to be the website's main attraction.
"This started as a joke between me and my friends, and thus when I started this website, I decided to just leave it in," he laughed.
"It essentially came because a friend joked that the haze made smoking technically less harmful as the difference between inhaled smoke and the surrounding air has decreased," he added.
Well, that's one way to look at it. Though, of course, smoking remains harmful no matter how hazy the air gets.
Who knew a joke among friends could turn into a haze tracker that thousands of Singaporeans would find useful?

mom.headline: Investigation outcome for alleged cheating and fraudulent work injury compensation claim involving EatGreen Pte Ltd
mom.teaser: The Singapore Police Force (SPF) and the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) have completed their investigations into a case of alleged cheating and fraudulent work injury compensation claim respectively, involving a former worker employed by EatGreen Pte. Ltd., which operates Sumo Salad.
